extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians, philosophers of mathematics, and researchers interested in mathematical practice and peer review (especially referees and editors)
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative standards and descriptive distinctions for when intentional gaps in ordinary (non-formal) mathematical proofs are acceptable in published practice, with attention to refereeing norms. The paper synthesizes interview and literature evidence to articulate criteria (e.g., types of gaps, expert-visibility) that govern acceptability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert-visibility criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: “The sorts of proof gaps that are acceptable are the ones that relevant experts can see and still be convinced” (Easwaran 2009, quoted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptability hinges on whether the intended expert readership can 'see' the skipped steps and still be convinced of the argument; gaps that are transparent to relevant experts are more likely to be acceptable. The paper's interviews support this picture.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refereeing limitation on intentional gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: “Mathematicians’ refereeing practices limit the number of certain intentional gaps in published proofs.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Referees play a gatekeeping role: they seriously assess whether a submission is sound and may require authors to fill gaps or, conversely, to remove excessive detail. Published acceptability of gaps is shaped by how referees respond to them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enthymematic gaps (omitted routine steps)
rubrics_metrics.description: Enthymematic gaps are routine or straightforward steps left out of proofs; the paper discusses their role in ordinary proofs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors commonly omit straightforward intermediate steps (enthymematic gaps). Referees may ask authors to provide less detail (i.e., leave more enthymematic gaps) in parts judged routine, or to add detail where necessary. The acceptability of these gaps depends on context and audience expertise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Untraversed and universally untraversed gaps (distinct gap types)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper treats distinctions among enthymematic gaps, untraversed gaps, and universally untraversed gaps and notes the need to clarify their relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These categories are used to classify types of omissions in proofs; the paper responds to referees' requests to clarify how these gap-types relate. Authors and referees should be attentive to which category a gap falls into when judging acceptability (e.g., whether a gap is expected to be easily 'traversed' by experts).

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper explicitness (avoid over-elaboration)
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoting Grice (via Paseau): 'Finicky over-elaboration of intervening steps is frowned upon... proper explicitness is an Aristotelian mean.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a balance between too little and too much explicitness. Over-elaboration of intermediate steps can be branded pedantry and is undesirable; authors should aim for the appropriate level of detail (neither excessive nor insufficient) given the audience and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rejection of probabilistic proofs as acceptable substitutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Easwaran (2009) account: mathematicians are generally unwilling to accept probabilistic proofs, even if they accept proofs that skip steps and are long/complicated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Skipping deductive steps that experts can follow is treated differently from offering probabilistic (non-deductive) arguments; probabilistic proofs typically do not meet standards of acceptability in mathematical practice discussed here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-formal/ordinary-proof standard (intuitive completeness suffices)
rubrics_metrics.description: The paper studies gaps in ordinary mathematical proofs (as they occur in practice), which are not formal proofs; an intuitive notion of a 'complete proof' is taken as sufficient for the analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating gaps in typical mathematical writing, one should not demand full formalization; instead use an ordinary-practice standard of completeness—i.e., whether the omitted steps are acceptable given informal norms and the intended expert readership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Context-dependence of thoroughness (role of activity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Interviews suggest mathematicians may be less thorough when not acting as referees, since referees take the task of determining whether the submitted paper is sound very seriously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acceptability of gaps varies with the social role and activity: authors, readers, and referees may apply different standards of scrutiny. The referee role typically invokes higher demands for detail to establish soundness.
